newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian exports drop, raise concerns on deficit.
newsitem.headline: Australian exports drop, raise concerns on deficit.

text.p: A large drop in export earnings for November saw Australia's current acount deficit rise to its highest level for a year on Monday and economists said the deficit might once again become a headache for the markets.
The current account deficit widened to A$1.923 billion (US$1.520 billion)in November, its highest level since November 1995, from A$1.807 billion in October, official figures showed.

"With the economy expected to recover over the course of 1997, we expect the current account deficit to continue to widen, largely on the back of the strength of imports," Bankers Trust Australia senior economist David Bassanese said.
Economists said while the deficit was not yet at problem levels, the fifth consecutive rise in the monthly deficit was not a good sign at a time when domestic activity was subdued.

"The first news for 1997 shows that the current account deficit is on the way up," State Bank of New South Wales chief economist Hans Kunnen said. "Granted, it is not yet at "problem" levels, but the direction is wrong," he said.

A 4.9 percent fall in exports, combined with an already published 1.2 percent rise in imports, saw the trade balance deteriorate by A$389 million to a A$394 million deficit in November, the largest trade shortfall since November 1995.
It was a cyclical improvement in the trade balance that lead to the improvement in current account deficit through 1996 from the record levels reached in the middle of 1995.
Analysts said that trend may be now coming to an end.

With the government forecasting business investment to grow at 14 percent in the current fiscal year, and 1996's three rate cuts expected to give economic growth and consumer spending a boost in 1997, the signs are pointing to a rising imports bill.
Rising business investment usually leads to higher imports, as Australia imports a lot of its capital goods, analysts said.

As well, exporters have been hurt by the Australian dollar's strength through 1996 -- it rose by over 20 percent against the Japanese yen and over seven percent against the U.S. dollar -- which has also improved the competitiveness of imports.

"If we do get these investment numbers realised and consumers start spending a little bit of money, we get a big rise in imports and the current account blows out again," Citibank Australia chief economist Stephen Koukoulas said.

Economists said any deterioration in the trade balance almost certainly meant a higher current account deficit because inroads were not expected to be made into the main component of the current account, the net income deficit, for some time yet.

The net income deficit, which represents debt and dividend payments to foreigners, has averaged A$1.7 billion over the first 11 months of 1996 and economists said they expected it to provide a medium-term floor under the current account.

"For both currency and credit markets, this means that, while the current account may not be the "bad" news story of 1997, it certainly won't be the "good" news story that it was in 1996," Commonwealth Bank economists said in a commentary.

Whatever happens over 1997, the news may be published in a different format. The Australian Bureau of Statistics said it was proposing to publish full current account data every quarter and a monthly trade report to improve accuracy.
